lead: Real gases do not obey μ = μ° + RT ln P, because their molecules attract and repel each other. Fugacity f is the corrected pressure that keeps the logarithmic form of the chemical potential exactly true. Its ratio to the true pressure, φ = f/P, is the fugacity coefficient, which measures how far the gas is from ideal. Every vapour-liquid equilibrium calculation in a simulator, every K-value, and every distillation column design rests on fugacity. This chapter defines f, shows how to compute φ from pressure-volume-temperature data, and extends both ideas to mixtures.
prereq: You need: chemical potential from Chapter 5.1, the compressibility factor and equations of state from Unit 2, and residual Gibbs energy from Unit 4.

blocks.text: For an ideal gas at fixed temperature, the chemical potential rises logarithmically with pressure: μ = μ°(T) + RT ln(P/P°). Doubling the pressure adds RT ln 2, about 1.7 kJ/mol at 300 K. The derivation assumes molecules do not interact and V = RT/P exactly.

A real gas breaks that assumption. Attraction pulls molecules together, so at moderate pressure the volume is smaller than RT/P, and the simple logarithm no longer gives the correct μ. G. N. Lewis (1901) kept the shape of the equation and replaced pressure by a corrected pressure, the fugacity.

blocks.where: μᵢ is the chemical potential of species i in J/mol; μᵢ° is its value in the reference state at the same T; R = 8.314 J/(mol·K); fᵢ is the fugacity in bar or Pa; fᵢ° is the fugacity of the reference state.

blocks.text: The definition is completed by a limiting condition: fᵢ → Pᵢ as P → 0, where Pᵢ is the partial pressure. At low pressure every gas becomes ideal, so fugacity and pressure merge there. The usual reference is the pure ideal gas at P° = 1 bar, for which f° = 1 bar. Then ln(fᵢ/fᵢ°) is simply ln(fᵢ / 1 bar), and fᵢ itself carries units of pressure.

blocks.where: φᵢ is the fugacity coefficient, dimensionless; Pᵢ is the partial pressure, yᵢP for a gas mixture or P for a pure gas. Some syllabi call φ the fugacity coefficient and write it as f/p.

blocks.text: φ → 1 as P → 0. An ideal gas has φ = 1 at every pressure, so any value away from 1 is a direct measure of non-ideality. Because at equilibrium a species has the same μ in every phase (Chapter 5.1), it also has the same fugacity in every phase at the same temperature and reference. That equality, not equality of pressures, is what Unit 6 solves for VLE.

At fixed temperature, dG = V dP for any fluid. For an ideal gas the same step gives dGⁱᵍ = (RT/P) dP. The difference between the real and ideal changes, integrated from zero pressure where the fluid is ideal, is the residual Gibbs energy: Gᴿ = RT ln φ for a pure fluid.

blocks.where: V is molar volume in m³/mol; R = 8.314 J/(mol·K); T in K; P in Pa; Z = PV/RT is the compressibility factor at the same T and P.

blocks.text: Read the sign. If Z < 1 the gas is more compressible than ideal, f is smaller than P and φ < 1. If Z > 1, φ > 1. The integrand (Z − 1)/P vanishes as P → 0 because Z → 1 there, so the integral converges. That is why the lower limit can be zero even though P appears in the denominator.

Two routes give the integral quickly. For moderate pressures use the truncated virial equation Z = 1 + BP/RT, which gives ln φ = BP/RT with B in m³/mol. For high pressures, use a cubic equation of state and integrate its Z, as covered in Unit 2.

items: Get Z at the given T for pressures from 0 (or 1 bar) up to the working pressure.
Form (Z − 1)/P at each pressure and integrate numerically or analytically.
Exponentiate the result to get φ.
Multiply by P to get f = φP, in the same pressure unit.

sections.h3: Mixtures, residual Gibbs energy and generalized correlation

blocks.text: In a mixture each species has its own fugacity f̂ᵢ, defined by the same equation μᵢ = μᵢ° + RT ln(f̂ᵢ/fᵢ°) with the same reference state. The corresponding coefficient is φ̂ᵢ = f̂ᵢ/Pᵢ = f̂ᵢ/(yᵢP), where yᵢ is the mole fraction in the gas. This is a partial molar property in the sense of Chapter 5.2, so the integration becomes ln φ̂ᵢ = (1/RT) ∫₀^P (V̄ᵢ − RT/P) dP, with V̄ᵢ the partial molar volume.

blocks.where: Gᴿ is the residual Gibbs energy of the mixture in J/mol; xᵢ is the mole fraction; φ̂ᵢ is the fugacity coefficient of species i in the mixture. For a pure fluid this reduces to ln φ = Gᴿ/RT.

blocks.text: An ideal solution obeys the Lewis-Randall rule f̂ᵢ = xᵢ fᵢ^pure, so φ̂ᵢ equals the pure-fluid φᵢ at the same T and P (see Chapter 5.5). Real mixtures deviate, and that deviation is what activity coefficients in Chapter 5.7 correct for.

Generalized correlation. Put the Pitzer virial form into the integral. With B⁰ = 0.083 − 0.422/Tᵣ^1.6 and B¹ = 0.139 − 0.172/Tᵣ^4.2, and BPc/RTc = B⁰ + ωB¹, where Tᵣ = T/Tc, Pᵣ = P/Pc and ω is the acentric factor, the result is ln φ = (Pᵣ/Tᵣ)(B⁰ + ωB¹). This needs only Tc, Pc and ω, and is reliable for non-polar gases up to a few bar.

examples.question: A pure gas at 10.0 bar has Z = 0.90, constant from 1.0 bar to 10.0 bar. Below 1.0 bar the gas is ideal. Taking the ideal-gas reference at 1.0 bar, estimate φ and f at 10.0 bar.
steps: Write the working formula: ln φ = ∫₀^P (Z − 1) dP/P. Below 1 bar, Z = 1, so the integrand is zero and that part adds nothing.
Substitute Z = 0.90 for the range 1.0 to 10.0 bar: ln φ = (0.90 − 1) ∫₁^10 dP/P = (−0.10) ln(10.0/1.0).
Exponentiate: φ = e^(−0.2303) = 0.7943. The value is below 1, as expected for Z < 1.
Convert to fugacity: f = φP = 0.7943 × 10.0 bar = 7.94 bar.
examples.answer: At 10.0 bar, φ = 0.794 and f = 7.94 bar, lower than the true pressure.
examples.check:
import math
Z = 0.90
P1 = 1.0
P2 = 10.0
lnphi = (Z - 1.0) * math.log(P2 / P1)
phi = math.exp(lnphi)
f = phi * P2
print(round(lnphi, 4))
print(round(phi, 4))
print(round(f, 3))

traps: Setting f = P for a real gas. That is true only in the ideal-gas limit; using it at 10 bar here would overstate the fugacity by 26 percent.
Mixing reference states. If f° is taken at 1 bar in one step and at the system pressure in the next, the RT ln term picks up a spurious offset.
Using log₁₀ instead of ln in ln φ = ∫(Z − 1) dP/P. The formula needs natural logarithms throughout.
Forgetting that a liquid or solid has a fugacity too, and it is not equal to the total pressure. For a liquid, f ≈ P^sat φ^sat times a Poynting correction.
Treating φ̂ᵢ of a mixture as the pure φᵢ at the same T and P without checking the Lewis-Randall assumption.

quiz.q: Define fugacity and fugacity coefficient for a pure gas.
quiz.a: Fugacity f is the corrected pressure defined by μ = μ° + RT ln(f/f°), with f → P as P → 0. The fugacity coefficient is φ = f/P, dimensionless, and φ → 1 as P → 0.

quiz.q: State the value of φ for an ideal gas at any pressure, and for any real gas as P → 0.
quiz.a: φ = 1 for an ideal gas at every pressure, and φ → 1 for any real gas as P → 0.

quiz.q: Why can μ = μ°(T) + RT ln P not be used for a real gas?
quiz.a: The logarithmic form follows from dG = V dP with V = RT/P. A real gas has V ≠ RT/P because of intermolecular forces, so the integrated expression is wrong. Fugacity replaces P by a corrected pressure so the same form stays exact, with all the correction carried inside f.

quiz.q: A gas has Z = 0.85 over a range of pressure. Is its fugacity larger or smaller than its pressure, and why?
quiz.a: Z < 1 makes (Z − 1)/P negative, so ln φ is negative, φ < 1 and f < P. The molecules attract each other, the gas escapes less strongly than an ideal gas would, so its effective pressure is lower than the true one.

quiz.q: A gas has Z = 0.95, constant from 1 bar to 8 bar, and is ideal below 1 bar. Find φ and f at 8 bar.
For a pure gas at 300 K and 10 bar, φ = 0.794. Find its residual Gibbs energy.
quiz.a: Gᴿ = RT ln φ = 8.314 × 300 × ln(0.794) = 2494.2 × (−0.2307) = −575 J/mol. The negative sign means the real gas has lower Gibbs energy than the ideal gas at the same T and P.

quiz.q: A binary gas mixture at 300 K has equal mole fractions with ln φ̂₁ = −0.10 and ln φ̂₂ = −0.30. Find Gᴿ of the mixture and say whether the mixture is ideal.
quiz.a: Gᴿ/RT = Σ xᵢ ln φ̂ᵢ = 0.5(−0.10) + 0.5(−0.30) = −0.20. Gᴿ = −0.20 × 8.314 × 300 = −499 J/mol. Gᴿ ≠ 0 and the two coefficients differ, so the mixture is not an ideal solution and the Lewis-Randall rule does not hold.

beyond: Not for the exam. Process simulators such as Aspen Plus and DWSIM compute φ̂ᵢ from an equation of state for every stage of every column, and the K-value is simply the ratio of liquid to vapour fugacity coefficients. Supercritical CO₂ extraction of caffeine from coffee beans, and CO₂ capture from flue gas, are designed entirely from fugacity coefficients near the critical point, where φ can drop well below 0.5. For dilute gases in water, Henry's law is really a statement about the fugacity of the dissolved species, so environmental models of dissolved oxygen in a lake use the same φ. Search terms to go further: Peng-Robinson fugacity coefficient, Poynting correction, Lewis fugacity rule, and fugacity of a solid.
